title: Bengio's LawZero lands up to CAD $300M from Canada and Germany
subtitle: A public-sector bet on "safe-by-design" AI backs a non-frontier lab pursuing Bengio's Scientist AI: transparent, evidence-based, no autonomous goals.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: LawZero, the Montreal-headquartered non-profit founded by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio, announced on September 16, 2026, a joint commitment of up to CAD $300 million in funding from the governments of Canada and Germany. The money will grow LawZero's international scientific team, secure world-class compute, and open a new office in Germany. In parallel, Bengio told AFP in an interview published the same week that humanity is "losing control" of AI and called for nuclear-arms-style safeguards on autonomous agents that can "get through cybersecurity barriers and enter any company."

The technical bet is a research program Bengio calls Scientist AI. The core idea is a model designed to reason transparently and output verifiable, evidence-based conclusions — without pursuing goals of its own. If the frontier labs are optimizing for capable agents that act in the world, LawZero is optimizing for capable non-agents that produce trustworthy explanations. It is a wager that a system without a goal is easier to keep aligned than one that has been trained to want things and then constrained. The scientific jury on that wager is still out; the funding buys time to run the experiment at meaningful scale.

The political story is the shape of the funders. Two national governments jointly backing an independent, non-commercial AI lab, at a scale that starts to compete with a frontier lab's compute budget, is a new template. Canada gets to matter in a field where its home-grown researchers seeded most of the modern deep-learning revolution. Germany gets a European AI-safety anchor that is neither French nor UK-affiliated. Whether other democracies co-fund — Japan, Australia, the Nordics — is the question that determines if LawZero becomes CERN for AI safety or stays a boutique.

Takeaway for learners: safety research is now a real career track, not a side interest. Read the LawZero technical papers, MILA's alignment publications, and Anthropic's interpretability work in parallel — they disagree in interesting ways. If you can explain three different definitions of alignment, name two published attacks on RLHF, and reproduce a simple mechanistic-interpretability finding on a small model, you are qualified to apply for entry-level roles in this field. It is still a small enough discipline that individual work is visible.
